Learning Objectives
Explain the pathomechanics contributing to hallux valgus deformity.
Understand the appropriate workup for patients with hallux valgus deformity, including
physical examination, and imaging studies, and recognition of concomitant deformities.
Discuss nonsurgical and surgical treatment options.
Describe treatment outcomes, surgical expectations, possible complications, and rationales to
ensure optimal results.

Hallux valgus deformity is commonly referred to as a bunion. The term bunion may have
originated in the early 18th century, ultimately deriving from Old French buignon, from
buigne, meaning bump on the head. Alternatively, an older etymology suggests the Latin
bunio, meaning turnip. Hallux valgus refers specifically to angulation of the first toe
metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint.
Epidemiology
Hallux valgus is defined as lateral deviation of the proximal phalanx on the first metatarsal
head.
It frequently is associated with medial deviation (varus) of the first metatarsal.
Hallux valgus is more common in women than in men.

Epidemiology
Forefoot pathology is common. In a large population study, more than 3,000 participants
were evaluated via physical examination, imaging studies, and dynamic foot pressure
studies.1 The aim of this study was to determine the incidence of foot pathology and
correlate it with functional foot shape and weight-bearing pressure maps. The authors of
the study reported that 65% of the participants had some foot pathology or symptoms,
many of which were in the forefoot. Hallux valgus was observed in 26% of the
participants, and lesser toe pathology was observed in 25% of the participants. Most
commonly, forefoot pathology did not occur in isolation. This study also assessed the
correlation between forefoot pathology and longitudinal arch mechanics. Correlations
were reported between forefoot deformities (hallux valgus and hammer toes) and pes
planus, and a negative correlation was found with cavus feet.
Although hallux valgus deformity is well identified, it often is minimally symptomatic.
Factors that appear to worsen symptoms include the amount of deformity, shoe
preferences, transfer metatarsalgia, and activity level.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
With valgus deviation of the great toe, the metatarsal assumes a varus position.
The sesamoid complex assumes a lateral position relative to the first metatarsal head, which is
shifted medially.
With progression, the windlass mechanism is lost, resulting in loss of weight bearing under the
first metatarsal and transfer to the lesser metatarsals (transfer metatarsalgia).
Vascular Anatomy
Terminal branches of the dorsalis pedis artery and the posterior tibial artery
Ankle-brachial index higher than 0.5; normal ankle-brachial index range is 0.9 to 1.3
Toe pressures normally are greater than 40 mm Hg
Transcutaneous oxygen pressure normally higher than 40 mm Hg; poor healing is associated
with a transcutaneous oxygen pressure lower than 30 mm Hg
Nerves
Five cutaneous nerves supply the forefoot.
Superficial peroneal: dorsal foot (medial and intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerves)
Deep peroneal: first web space
Sural: lateral border of the foot (lateral dorsal cutaneous nerve)
Tibial: plantar foot (medial and lateral plantar nerves)
Saphenous: medial border of the foot
Terminal branches of the saphenous and superficial peroneal sensory nerves may be
compressed over the medial eminence.
Tendons
Dorsal extensor tendons: extensor hallucis longus and brevis
Plantar tendons from medial to lateral forming the plantar plate
Abductor hallucis
Flexor hallucis brevis medial head and sesamoid
Flexor hallucis longus
Flexor hallucis brevis lateral head and sesamoid

Adductor hallucis oblique head followed by the transverse head
The adductor tendon, via its insertion on the proximal phalanx and the fibular sesamoid,
becomes a deforming force.
Joints and Ligaments
MTP articulation
Metatarsosesamoidal articulation
Medial and lateral collateral ligaments originating from the midportion of the metatarsal head
The plantar plate of the first MTP joint includes the sesamoid bones and a dense fibrous
sheath, which has attachments to the plantar intrinsics, the intermetatarsal ligament, and the
plantar aponeurosis.
The medial capsule of the MTP joint becomes attenuated, and the lateral capsule contracts.
Musculature
The adductor brevis is a deforming force.
With advanced sesamoid displacement, the flexor hallucis longus also becomes a deforming
force.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The mechanics of the first MTP joint are complex. Although three muscles attach to the
proximal phalanx and two muscles attach to the distal phalanx, no muscles attach to the
metatarsal head. Therefore, the metatarsal head exists in a dynamic equilibrium
between these distal lines of pull and the joint reactive forces at the
metatarsosesamoidal articulation.
As the hallux rotates into a valgus and pronated position, numerous anatomic
relationships change, ultimately leading to deformity progression. The exact pathologic
cascade resulting in a valgus and pronated hallux is unclear but involves the following
process. The static stabilizers around the first MTP joint attenuate or fail (especially the
medial collateral ligament), permitting medial translation of the metatarsal head and
varus of the metatarsal shaft. The lateral capsule structures contract, creating a static
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:20 PM
AAOS | Hallux Valgus: Disorders of the First Ray
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000500
4/23

deforming force. As the metatarsal head drifts medially, the sesamoids, anchored by the
adductor hallucis and the intermetatarsal ligament, drift over the crista. This may occur
with or without corresponding metatarsal and hallux pronation.
As the hallux moves into valgus and/or pronation, the muscle vectors that previously
stabilized the MTP joint accentuate the deformity.
Recently, weight-bearing CT has been used to demonstrate the true three-dimensional
complexity of this pathology. A study comparing control participants and patients with
hallux valgus found that first metatarsal and phalangeal pronation did not correlate with
the first-second intermetatarsal angle (IMA1-2) or the hallux valgus angle (HVA).2 A similar
study documented the complex relationship between pronation and sesamoid
subluxation.3 Most patients had both deformities; however, 13% of the patients had no
pronation deformity, and 38% of the patients had no sesamoid subluxation, highlighting
that lateralization of the sesamoid position does not necessarily occur with metatarsal
varus alone.
Etiology
Symptomatic hallux valgus commonly is related to wearing shoes that have a narrow toe box.
Metatarsus primus varus and pes planus have been implicated in hallux valgus.
Of patients with hallux valgus, 70% have a family history of the condition, which suggests a
hereditary component.
Other causes include rheumatoid arthritis, connective tissue disorders, trauma, and cerebral
palsy.
The metatarsal articular surface may have a valgus (lateral) orientation, as measured by the
distal metatarsal articular angle (DMAA), which may contribute to hallux valgus deformity
(especially with juvenile deformity).
Natural History
Usually slow progression of the deformity
Subluxation of the MTP joint is associated with more rapid worsening.

Risk Factors
Hereditary
In women, associated with a normal body mass index and high heel use, beginning at age 20
years
In men, associated with higher body mass index and pes planus
Classification
Informally categorized as mild, moderate, and severe
Additional variables include age, hyperflexibility, congruency of the MTP joint, and arthritis.

Classification
Classification of bunion deformity is difficult because a continuum of severity exists and
discrete elements of the deformity may not change in a uniform manner. Usually, the
deformity progresses over time; however, progression is variable. The separate
components of the deformity change at different rates or may not worsen over time. For
example, angular measurements will worsen in combination with degenerative changes.
Conversely, an abnormal DMAA or joint laxity may remain constant.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Pain over the medial eminence
Difficulty with narrow shoes
Changes in activity level
Worsening alignment
Transfer metatarsalgia
Impingement of the hallux on the second toe
Physical Examination

A bony prominence may be noted along the medial aspect of the first MTP joint.
The patient may report pain along the prominence with shoe wear.
Swelling and redness may result from bursal inflammation.
Calluses may develop on the plantarmedial aspect of the first MTP and the first
interphalangeal joints.
Nerve tenderness may be present with compression of the digital nerves.
Signs of stress transfer laterally to the second MTP joint.
Second MTP deviation, second hammer toe, and impingement calluses

Physical Examination
In describing symptoms, patients most frequently localize pain to the medial aspect of
the first MTP joint (the medial eminence). As many as one-half of patients also may
describe pain at the plantar aspect of the lesser MTP joints secondary to transfer
metatarsalgia. Symptoms are commonly exacerbated by shoe wear and may improve if
the patient is barefoot.
Physical examination should be performed with the patient standing and sitting, with
observation of the deformity and change with weight-bearing. A standard neurovascular
examination should be performed. The foot and ankle are then carefully palpated, and
range of motion is globally assessed. At the first MTP joint, particular attention is paid to
the passive reducibility of deformity and to evaluation for coexisting pain and/or crepitus
(end range and mid arc). Tarsometatarsal (TMT) stability should be assessed in every
patient. The lateral forefoot is stabilized with one hand and the first ray is manipulated
with the other hand. Dorsoplantar translation and mediolateral translation can be
assessed.
Neurovascular Examination
Pulses and skin appearance
Rule out peripheral neuropathy, especially in patients with diabetes mellitus
Muscular spasticity may influence surgical outcomes.

Imaging Studies
After physical examination, weight-bearing radiographs (AP, oblique, and lateral views)
are obtained. The IMA1-2, HVA, hallux valgus interphalangeus angle, and DMAA are
measured. MTP joint space and congruency are then assessed, and roundedness of the
lateral metatarsal head is characterized to assess for pronation deformity. The position
and degree of sesamoid subluxation/dislocation also is evaluated, with the
understanding that lateral displacement of the sesamoids may be true subluxation or
pseudo-subluxation. On lateral radiographs, the TMT joint is inspected for plantar
gapping and dorsal subluxation; however, gapping has not been correlated with
measurable hypermobility. Although weight-bearing CT aids in visualizing and
understanding the hallux valgus deformity, no evidence shows that weight-bearing CT
enhances surgical correction or improves patient outcomes.
Pathology
Medial capsule attenuation
Plantarlateral migration of the abductor hallucis causes a change in force from abduction to
plantar flexion and pronation.
Stretching of the extensor hood and lateral subluxation of the extensor tendons accentuate
valgus deformity.
Medial displacement of the metatarsal head relative to the sesamoids
Imbalanced pull of the adductor hallucis
Contracture of the lateral capsule
Diagnosis
Components of the deformity to consider include the following:
IMA (amount of metatarsal varus and general width of the foot)
Hallux valgus angle (measures toe deviation)
Hallux valgus interphalangeus

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management includes shoe-wear modifications, including the use of shoes with a
wide toe box and soft uppers.
Occasionally, pads or cushions over the prominence can help relieve pain related to hallux
valgus.
Orthoses may be helpful in patients with pes planus or symptoms of metatarsalgia.
Activity modifications
Nonsurgical management may afford symptomatic relief but will not correct the deformity.
Setting expectations for nonsurgical and surgical management is critical.
Indications
Pain over the first MTP joint medial eminence
Painful impingement of the hallux against the second toe


Techniques/Procedures
Numerous osteotomies and corrective procedures have been documented, and the
surgeon should select the procedure that works well and reproducibly best serves each
patient. Management should include a three-dimensional focus for deformity correction,
AP deformity correction, and axial positioning of the sesamoids.4 The following
framework is used to guide surgical decision making.
In patients with substantial MTP joint arthrosis, arthrodesis should be considered.
Cronin et al5 documented secondary corrections of IMA1-2 without additional
procedures. For fixation options, several methods have been described. The most
common procedure includes preparing the joint surfaces via hemispherical reamers and
dorsal fixation with the use of a contoured plate.
In patients with a preserved and congruent MTP joint, the first step is to determine if the
deformity can be corrected via distal osteotomies. For mild deformities (HVA <30°, IMA1-
2 <13°, DMAA <15°), a biplanar chevron osteotomy at the distal metatarsal can be
performed. The most popular technique is described by Saltzman et al.6 If residual
deformity or hallux valgus interphalangeus is present, an Akin osteotomy at the proximal
phalanx can be added. Collectively, these procedures can correct as much as
approximately 4° in the IMA1-2, 14° in the HVA, and 7° in the DMAA. Patient satisfaction
with this technique is between 80% and 95%.6,7 The primary disadvantage of this
approach is that the pronation deformity is not addressed, which may make reduction of
the sesamoids a challenge even after distal soft-tissue release. For congruent joints with
larger deformities, patients may require a distal metatarsal osteotomy to correct an
increased DMAA and more proximal correction to correct the larger IMA.

In patients with a preserved but incongruent MTP joint and mild deformity (HVA <30°,
IMA1-2 <13°), many surgeons perform a chevron osteotomy. Occasionally, a limited distal
soft-tissue procedure also is performed to improve joint congruency. Other approaches,
such as a scarf osteotomy or a more proximal metatarsal osteotomy, have been
described; however, no conclusive evidence has identified any one approach to be
superior. The surgeon should carefully consider the limitations of each technique in each
patient. For example, biplanar chevron and scarf osteotomies will not correct large
pronation deformities, and a supinating osteotomy or first TMT joint fusion may be more
appropriate.
In patients with a preserved but incongruent MTP joint and moderate deformity (HVA
<40°, IMA1-2 13° to 20°), a more proximal osteotomy or a first TMT joint arthrodesis is
required. Numerous proximal osteotomies have been described, including a lateral
closing or medial opening wedge osteotomy, scarf osteotomy, Ludloff osteotomy,
crescentic osteotomy, and proximal rotational osteotomy. If the deformity involves
substantial pronation and/or TMT joint instability, many surgeons prefer a Lapidus
procedure. For a proximal metatarsal osteotomy, a medial opening wedge osteotomy is
simple and reproducible and can be well secured with the use of a low-profile medial
locking plate.
In patients with a preserved but incongruent MTP joint and severe deformity (HVA >40°,
IMA1-2 >20°), arthrodesis of the TMT joint or the first MTP joint is required. The more
severe the deformity, the more likely the author of this lesson is to suggest first MTP
fusion as a more predictable means of deformity correction. These procedures allow for
powerful correction in multiple planes, including rotation. Although earlier clinical series
on the Lapidus procedure have reported a high nonunion rate (almost 10%), modern
fixation and fusion techniques have resulted in much lower nonunion rates (4% to 5%).8
Minimally invasive incision techniques have been described. Concerns for a high
complication rate exist.9

Surgical Approaches
Medial midline approach favored over dorsomedial approach (avoids cutaneous nerves)
The Lapidus procedure can be performed via a single extended medial incision or two
separate incisions.
An incision often is made in the web space between the first and second metatarsals.
Postoperative Management
Depending on the procedure, off-loading the first MTP joint immediately postoperatively may
be important. Some procedures allow for immediate–weight bearing, depending on technique
and fixation.
Osteotomy and arthrodesis procedures require an initial period of immobilization and non–
weight bearing.
Modern fixation techniques allow for earlier weight bearing.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Managing expectations

Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Numerous complications can occur after the surgical management of hallux valgus.10
Potential complications should be discussed with the patient in detail preoperatively to
set expectations appropriately.11 One of the most frequent complications is stiffness. A
cadaver model study reported a 23° decrease in MTP joint dorsiflexion after proximal
metatarsal osteotomy with distal soft-tissue reconstruction, emphasizing the importance
of early postoperative joint mobilization.12 Other complications include neurologic
sequelae (paresthesias, neuroma, sensory loss), transfer metatarsalgia in shortening
osteotomies, nonunion at an osteotomy or fusion site, recurrence, and hallux varus.
Although recurrence rates at long-term follow-up may be modest, recurrence is not
always associated with impaired function and pain. In patients with symptomatic
